claims.text: Eutectic high-entropy alloys can have a lamellar microstructure of alternating soft FCC and hard BCC/B2 phases.
AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is an example of an eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar FCC/B2 microstructure.
The soft and hard phases develop different oxide films at elevated temperature.
The phase-specific oxide film is poorly adherent and undergoes mechanically induced spallation during sliding.
Oxide spallation exposes a chemically active substrate.
The freshly exposed substrate promotes micro-galvanic corrosion at interfaces between the phases.
Phase-dependent, non-uniform oxide films and lamellar microstructural heterogeneity create local galvanic cells at phase boundaries.
Differential corrosion kinetics between adjacent phases weaken the oxide and underlying substrate.
Repeated oxide disruption, corrosion, and oxide reformation form a positive-feedback cycle that intensifies both wear and localized corrosion.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature produce significantly greater total material loss than isolated wear or isolated corrosion.
Coupled exposure increases corrosion current density and pitting depth relative to corrosion without mechanical disruption.
Coupled exposure increases wear-track volume loss relative to wear in an inert environment.
In the absence of mechanical wear, a continuous and more protective oxide layer can form on this eutectic HEA.
Temperatures of approximately 600–800 °C cause sufficiently rapid oxide growth and poor oxide adhesion for the proposed mechanism to become significant.
The proposed synergistic effect should be minimal or absent in inert environments.
The proposed synergistic effect should be minimal or absent at room temperature or in truly uniform single-phase alloys.
Oxidative wear can occur in a multiphase AlCoCrFeNiMoTi-based HEA coating.
A controlled comparison can use the same eutectic HEA under simultaneous wear-corrosion, corrosion without appreciable wear, and wear in an inert atmosphere at the same temperature.
Wear volume, corrosion current density, oxide integrity, and pit depth are measurable responses for testing the hypothesis.
Failure to observe statistically significant increases in total degradation and in the separate wear and corrosion indicators under coupled exposure would falsify the proposed mechanism.
